topic: Compile-Time vs. Runtime Polymorphism with Template Metaprogramming and Virtual Functions
explanation: This example explores the differences between compile-time polymorphism achieved through template metaprogramming and runtime polymorphism using virtual functions.  We'll examine how compilers handle each approach, impacting memory layout, performance, and the generated assembly code.  Compile-time polymorphism resolves function calls at compile time, leading to potentially faster execution and smaller code size but less flexibility. Runtime polymorphism, using virtual functions and vtables, introduces runtime overhead but allows for greater flexibility (e.g., adding new classes at runtime).
syntax: C++ Templates, Virtual Functions, and Inheritance
code_example: virtual void process() { std::cout << "Base class" << std::endl; }
void process() override { std::cout << "Derived class" << std::endl; }
std::cout << "Runtime polymorphism execution time: " << duration.count() << " microseconds\n";
example_explanation: The template example demonstrates compile-time polymorphism. The compiler generates separate code for each instantiation of `StaticPolymorphism`. There's no runtime overhead for function call resolution; the compiler directly chooses the correct function based on the template argument.  The virtual function example demonstrates runtime polymorphism. The compiler generates a vtable for each class with virtual functions. At runtime, the program uses the vtable to look up and execute the correct function, causing a slight performance overhead.  The assembly generated for the template case will directly call the appropriate `process` function (e.g., for int or double), while the virtual function example will involve an indirect function call through the vtable.  The runtime difference, though small in this simple example, could become significant with many calls and larger classes.  Memory layout is impacted, as each class with virtual functions has an additional pointer to its vtable.
